item.title: Install on Linux with Docker Swarm
item.description:
This page deploys CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Linux: one service for each resource class, and a clean container for every job. The steps cover one node (Multi-Node Clusters adds more). For a first run, Quickstart on Linux is shorter.

Note

If you can run Kubernetes, CircleCI recommends container runner for containerized jobs, and documents a plain machine runner 3 on Docker setup. This page is for teams that run Docker Swarm and want a clean container for every job.

Status. This is a CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, and CircleCI support does not cover it. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only: What is tested says how. Replicas are fixed: the stack does not add or remove nodes, and it does not scale to the queue.

Nothing is installed on a node by hand: a service of the stack installs the runner on every node, so docker stack deploy is the whole install. The optional setup helper runs the same steps.

Prerequisites

  • A CircleCI cloud organization and a user who is an organization admin. CircleCI server is not tested: CircleCI server says what is known.
  • The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, signed in. Pass --org <org> (a slug such as gh/my-org, or a UUID): without it the CLI uses the organization of the git remote of the current directory, which in a clone of this repository is not yours.
  • Docker Engine 24 or later, running, with Swarm mode (Podman cannot run Swarm). Root access or membership of the docker group, which is equivalent to root: limit it to administrators.
  • A node clock synchronized with NTP. TLS to CircleCI fails silently when the clock drifts.
  • Outbound HTTPS from each node to the hosts in Egress hosts: the release bucket of CircleCI (the runner), and the registries of the alpine image (the distributor) and the token proxy image (Docker Hub). No inbound access is needed. What needs internet lists everything. Not tested without internet access: Run the downloads from a mirror.
  • CPU and memory: the shipped file reserves 4 CPUs and 8 GB in total, and replicas that do not fit stay pending (Size the limits).
  • Runner concurrency in your CircleCI plan for your replicas (Capacity and concurrency).
Operating system Architecture Status in this repository
Ubuntu LTS amd64, arm64 Tested in CI on Ubuntu 26.04. On arm64, every pipeline checks that the stack installs the runner and starts, and probe jobs run on a real arm64 runner on main and smr-swarm/* branches
RHEL 8 and later, and compatible distributions amd64, arm64 Steps documented, not tested in CI
Any of the above ppc64le, s390x CI only starts the distributor and the token proxy image under emulation: no job has run on them

Self-hosted runner terms agreement

An organization admin must agree to the CircleCI Runner Terms before you install self-hosted runners through the web app. Through the CLI, you agree by installing and using them (details). Whether the token proxy between your runners and CircleCI is covered is for your own review: this project does not give legal advice.

Get the files

Use a release (recommended) or clone the repository at a release tag. Paths on this page are relative to the root of the repository or of the extracted bundle.

git clone --branch <release-tag> https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm.git
cd machine-runner-swarm

A release is recommended because its stack files name the token proxy image of that release by tag and digest. A clone names the tag latest, which is not a pin (The token proxy image). Each GitHub release carries four files, with <version> the release number without the v:

File Content
machine-runner-swarm-<version>.tar.gz The Linux bundle: stack files, scripts, documentation and examples, without the tests, plus VERSION and CHANGELOG.md
machine-runner-swarm-<version>.zip The same bundle for Windows
SHA256SUMS The SHA-256 checksum of both bundles
SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json A keyless cosign signature of SHA256SUMS

Verify a release

CircleCI signs SHA256SUMS with the OIDC token of the CircleCI job that makes the release. No signing key is stored anywhere. The signature proves that a job of this CircleCI project made the file, and the checksums prove that your download is the file the job made. You need cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested), curl, jq, and GNU coreutils, in a bash shell. On Windows, refer to Verify a release.

Set version once to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The download fails while the placeholder is unchanged.

version=X.Y.Z

Then paste this block. It runs in a subshell and stops at the first failing check. Only a bundle that passes the signature, the ref and the checksum is unpacked.

(
 set -euo pipefail
 base="https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v${version}"
 curl -fsSLO "${base}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" \
 -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS" \
 -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json"

 # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS
 cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
 --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \
 --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com"

 # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main
 # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main)
 hex=$(jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
 | base64 -d | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
 grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' <<< "${hex}" \
 && echo "signed for refs/heads/main" || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop"; exit 1; }

 # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list
 sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing

 # only a verified bundle is unpacked
 tar -xzf "machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz"
 echo "RELEASE VERIFIED"
)

Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files, and start again or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block reads the certificate extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) and fails unless its value is refs/heads/main. The pattern starts on a byte boundary, and ASN.1 tag 0c or 13 is the string type of the value.

Then change into the bundle:

cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}"

The token proxy image has its own signature: Verify the token proxy image has the commands.

The checks establish less than a review does. A valid signature and refs/heads/main mean that a job of this CircleCI project ran for the main branch and made these files. Whether anyone can change main without a review is a setting of the organization that owns the repository, which this page cannot check (A ruleset for main says what the project asks for).

  • The identity is the CircleCI project (7bbdbb66-...) and the pipeline definition (8b2a66db-...) that run this repository’s pipeline. The issuer https://oidc.circleci.com is the CircleCI OIDC issuer. Sigstore records every signature in a public transparency log.

  • To see the ref of a certificate, print it. The last line ends with the ref, and a release comes from refs/heads/main.

    jq -r '.verificationMaterial.certificate.rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | base64 -d \
 | openssl x509 -inform DER -noout -text | grep -A1 '1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14:'

  • If the project or its pipeline definition is ever re-created, the definition ID changes, and this page gives the new value.

The token proxy image

The token proxy is the one container that holds your class tokens (The token proxy). It is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs), which the stack file pulls on deploy. The name is not the trust root: the signature check of Verify the token proxy image is. It is a static Go binary that runs as a non-root user with a read-only root file system, and one tag covers linux/amd64, linux/arm64, linux/ppc64le and linux/s390x. Windows nodes get the Windows image from the same tag (Windows).

Tag What it is
X.Y.Z The image of a release. It never changes: pin this one
X.Y, X The newest release of that minor or major line
latest The newest release. The default of the stack files in a checkout, and only a release moves it
edge The newest commit of the main branch that passed the end-to-end tests. For testing main, not for jobs that matter
sha-<12 characters> One commit of the main branch, published before its tests have run

The stack file reads the image from MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE. A release bundle defaults to ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:<version>@sha256:<digest>, a checkout to ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:latest (linux/setup.sh --deploy warns when the variable is not pinned by digest). To use another image (a digest for a pin, a registry of your own for an air gap, a local build for development), set the variable in the environment of docker stack deploy. The image must be on the node that runs the proxy, so build a local one there, or copy it with docker save.

docker build -t machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev proxy/
sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

Upgrade the token proxy says how to change its tag.

1. Create the resource classes

  1. Create a namespace if your organization has none. An organization has one namespace, and orbs use the same one.

    circleci namespace create <namespace> --org <org>

  2. Create one resource class for each service in the stack file. The class name must equal the service name. The shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml has one service, linux-default: keep that name for a first run.

    circleci runner resource-class create <namespace>/linux-default --org <org> --generate-token

The command prints a token once: store it in your secret manager. If you lose it, run circleci runner token create <namespace>/<class> --nickname <nickname>. To rename the service, edit your copy of the file first (step 5), then create the class and the secret under the new name. More classes: Resource Classes.

2. Prepare each node

Run these steps on every node that runs services. A single node needs no firewall change. Multi-node clusters open the ports in Inter-node ports.

Ubuntu

  1. Install Docker Engine from Docker’s repository: Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu.

  2. Start the engine and confirm it runs.

    sudo systemctl enable --now docker
docker version

  3. Confirm the clock is synchronized. The command prints yes.

    timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value

RHEL

  1. Install Docker Engine from Docker’s repository: Install Docker Engine on RHEL. The Podman packages of RHEL cannot run Swarm.
  2. Do steps 2 and 3 of Ubuntu.
  3. Keep SELinux enforcing. The runner is in a Docker volume, so no host directory needs a label.

Note

CI does not run on RHEL, so these steps follow Docker’s documentation and have not been exercised in this repository.

3. Start Swarm

Run every docker command in these steps with sudo, or as a user in the docker group. On a single node, start Swarm on the loopback address only, so nothing is exposed to the network.

docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 --listen-addr 127.0.0.1:2377
docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2

The second command keeps fewer stopped containers on the node (each finished job leaves one until Swarm prunes its task). setup.sh --swarm-init runs both.

The node is a manager, and the token proxy runs on a manager by default. On a single node, set no proxy label. In a cluster, label the node that runs the proxy: runner services never run on a node with this label, so a job never shares a node with the proxy.

docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <manager node name>

With several managers, also pin the proxy to one (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). A loopback node cannot accept other nodes: for a cluster, use a routable address (Multi-Node Clusters).

4. Create the secrets

Create one secret for each service in the stack file, named <service>-token. It is a runner config file that holds only the token:

api:
 auth_token: <token>

The token proxy mounts these secrets at /run/secrets/<service>-token (uid 65534, mode 0400), and the runners never see them. The runners read one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token in the same format, mounted at /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml (runner user, uid 2000, mode 0400). Only the persistent class mounts its own token in the runner. Every other runner setting is a CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* variable in the stack file.

Set classes to every class you deploy. The loop asks for each token with a hidden prompt, so the token does not reach your shell history or the process list. It works in bash, zsh and dash and stops at an empty token. Do not use read -rsp: zsh reads -p as a coprocess, which leaves TOKEN empty and creates a secret without a token.

classes="linux-default"
for class in $classes; do
 printf 'Token for %s (hidden): ' "$class"
 stty -echo; IFS= read -r TOKEN; stty echo; echo
 [ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "no token entered for $class" >&2; break; }
 printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create "$class-token" -
done
unset TOKEN
printf 'api:\n auth_token: machine-runner-swarm-placeholder\n' | docker secret create runner-placeholder-token -

docker stack deploy fails with secret not found when a service references a missing secret: create every secret the file references, or delete the services you do not need from your copy. docker stack config prints the mode 0400 as 256.

5. Review the stack file

Copy linux/stack to a directory of your own, deploy/, and keep it under version control. From here on you check and deploy your copy and never the shipped files. For a first run, change nothing.

cp -r linux/stack deploy

Check that the file parses. This needs no running Swarm.

docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null

The directory holds the stack files and the two scripts that they ship as Swarm configs, circleci-runner-entrypoint and runner-distributor.sh. Keep the scripts next to the stack files, and keep the service runner-distributor and the top-level configs: and volumes:. A Swarm config cannot change, so its name carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its file: if you edit a script, rename its config the same way (sha256sum <file> | cut -c1-12).

Review these settings first (Resource Classes has the details):

Setting Default Change it to
Service name linux-default Your resource class name
image cimg/base:2026.10 Your image, pinned by digest (Images)
deploy.replicas 2 The number of concurrent jobs you need
deploy.resources 2 CPUs and 4 GB The size of one runner. Limits and reservations are equal
placement.constraints node.platform.os == linux Add architecture or zone constraints
x-distributor-env An exact runner version (3.1.13 in this release) with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, major version 3, a check every 24 hours Nothing for a first run. A newer pin, a floating version or a mirror are variables of docker stack deploy (Upgrade the runner on Linux)

The optional classes are add-on files in deploy/. Add each with another -c flag, and pass the same list on every deploy (how the files merge). Each needs its own resource class and secret <service>-token.

File Services Purpose
classes-extra.yaml linux-java, linux-hardened Examples: an image swap, and a class without sudo. Reserves 6 more CPUs and 12 GB (Define a class)
docker-build.yaml linux-docker-build Builds images with the host engine. Needs a labeled worker (Docker Builds)
microvm.yaml linux-microvm, linux-microvm-docker, microvm-dns Each job in a Kata Containers microVM. Needs KVM (MicroVM jobs)
persistent.yaml linux-persistent A long-lived runner. Needs the node name edited in the file (Persistent mode)
ssh-rerun.yaml linux-default-ssh Rerun job with SSH. Publishes port 54782 (Rerun job with SSH)

An add-on file repeats the common settings of runners.yaml (YAML anchors do not cross files), so it also loads alone. Change a common setting, such as stop_grace_period or the logging options, in every file that you use.

6. Deploy the stack

Deploy your copy from step 5. The command returns before the replicas run, because docker stack deploy does not wait.

docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

To add optional classes, pass your copies with more -c flags, and pass the same list on every later deploy:

docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/persistent.yaml runners

This is the whole install. The service runner-distributor starts on every Linux node, also on a node that joins later (not on a microVM node: its classes download their own runner). It downloads the runner version the stack file pins (the newest that CI tests), checks its SHA-256 against the values the stack file carries, and puts it in the volume runner-bin of the node. The service token-proxy pulls its image from Docker Hub. A runner container that starts first waits up to 120 seconds for the runner.

Other distributor settings, such as a floating version like 3.1 (weaker: the distributor trusts the manifest and ignores the default SHA-256 list), are variables of this command. sudo drops the environment: write sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 docker stack deploy ... (Upgrade the runner on Linux).

Verify the deployment

  1. List the services. Each shows the running and desired replicas.

    docker stack services runners
    ID NAME MODE REPLICAS IMAGE
... runners_linux-default replicated 2/2 cimg/base:2026.10
... runners_runner-distributor global 1/1 alpine:3
... runners_token-proxy replicated 1/1 ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:...

    The distributor has one task for each Linux node (a microVM node has none): 1/1 on one node, 3/3 on three.

  2. Check the tasks. A task in the Running state is a runner that polls CircleCI.

    docker service ps runners_linux-default

  3. Check that the distributor installed the runner. Its log has a line such as runner-distributor: [ ok ] current -> versions/3.1.13: circleci-runner 3.1.13 linux/amd64 for each node (See what runs).

    docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor

  4. Check that the runners connected. Each replica is listed as online, named <node hostname>-<service>-<slot> (for example node1-linux-default-1). The web app shows the same under Runners.

    circleci runner instance list --org <org> --resource-class <namespace>/linux-default

  5. Run a job with examples/linux-hello.yml (the quickstart shows it), twice. After each job, Swarm shows a new task for the slot. The job clean-check in examples/linux-jobs.yml fails if anything from an earlier job is still present.

Optional: use the setup helper

linux/setup.sh runs the steps above with checks. It never prints the token, every step is idempotent, and it needs bash 4.4 or later. It installs nothing on a node: the service runner-distributor installs the runner.

Step Effect
--check Preflight: Linux on amd64, arm64, ppc64le or s390x, Docker running and 24 or later, Swarm state, NTP
--swarm-init Runs docker swarm init on the loopback address unless Swarm is active, and sets the task history limit to 2
--secret <service> Creates the secret <service>-token from a token read on stdin
--deploy Runs docker stack deploy with each --stack-file. Without one it deploys the shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml, so pass your copy from step 5. It warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest

With no step it runs --check. Steps run in the order of the table. Options are --stack-file (repeatable) and --stack-name. Each run ends with Next: and the steps still to do, or Check: and the commands that show the runners start.

sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init
sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default
printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder
sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml
  • --secret asks for the token with a hidden prompt. To script it, pipe the token (printf %s "$TOKEN" | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default). Several --secret values need a terminal. A token has only letters, digits, ., _ and -, and an existing secret stays unchanged (Rotate a runner token). Create a secret for every service you deploy.
  • The helper does not label nodes. For a docker-build class, run docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true <worker node>.
  • The distributor reads MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 from the environment of --deploy, and the token proxy reads MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_*. sudo drops the environment: use sudo env VAR=value linux/setup.sh --deploy (Upgrade the runner on Linux).

Upgrade

The nodes keep the runner version that the stack file pins until you change it: Upgrade the runner and images covers versions, images and rollback.

A new release of this repository changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy/ is not updated by itself. To merge:

  1. Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.

  2. Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old directory is the base of the merge (for a cloned tag, use git worktree or a second clone).

  3. See what changed between the two releases.

    diff -ru "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack" "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack"

  4. Merge each file that differs into your copy. The command edits the file in place, marks conflicts with <<<<<<< lines, and exits with the number of conflicts.

    git merge-file deploy/runners.yaml \
 "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack/runners.yaml" \
 "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack/runners.yaml"

    Repeat for the other files you copied. Take the entrypoint and the distributor script of the new release unless you edited them, and rename their Swarm configs as Upgrade to a new release of this repository says.

  5. Check deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints and deploy.resources, the runner version pin with its SHA-256 values (a release changes them together), and the token proxy image (a release names it by digest).

  6. Check the result.

    docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null

  7. Deploy with the same list of -c files as before.

    docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

Swarm replaces the token proxy and updates the runner services one replica at a time. While the proxy is replaced, no new job is claimed, and every runner that had already claimed stays refused (Restart the proxy). To roll back, deploy the previous copy.

Stop and uninstall

Refer to Uninstall.

Troubleshooting

Refer to Troubleshooting. The most common problems on a first install are a missing secret, a node whose distributor cannot download the runner, and a task that stays pending because no node matches its constraints.

Additional resources

  • Concepts
  • Resource Classes
  • Security
  • Operations
  • Machine runner 3 configuration reference

item.title: Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm
item.description:
This page deploys CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server. Every job runs in a new Windows Server Core container, and Swarm replaces the container after the job. The steps cover one host (Multi-Node Clusters adds more). For a first run, Quickstart on Windows Server is shorter.

Note

If you can run Kubernetes, CircleCI recommends container runner for containerized jobs. This page is for teams that run Docker Swarm and need a clean Windows container for every job.

Status. This is a CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, and CircleCI support does not cover it. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only: What is tested says how. Replicas are fixed: the stack does not add or remove nodes, and it does not scale to the queue.

The steps: start or join a swarm, label the node, create the secrets, deploy. The optional setup helper runs most of them.

Important

The services run the stock Server Core image, and no image is built. Stopping a busy container from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds, so change a Windows class while it is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).

Prerequisites

  • A CircleCI cloud organization and a user who is an organization admin. CircleCI server is not tested: CircleCI server says what is known.
  • The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, signed in. It can run on your workstation. Pass --org <org> (a slug such as gh/my-org, or a UUID): without it the CLI uses the organization of the git remote of the current directory, which in a clone of this repository is not yours.
  • One or more Windows Server hosts (table below). The host cannot be a domain controller.
  • Docker Engine 28.0 or later (CLI and engine), in Windows-container mode, with the Windows Containers feature (enabling it restarts the host). The stack files mount a subpath of a volume (current and git\current), which older CLIs and engines ignore: the runner would not start. CI runs Docker 29.4.0 on Windows, and windows\Setup.ps1 checks the version. The Install-DockerCE script in the helpful_tools directory of the Microsoft Windows Containers repository installs both.
  • An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session.
  • A host clock synchronized with NTP. TLS to CircleCI fails silently when the clock drifts.
  • Outbound HTTPS from each host to the hosts in Egress hosts: circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com (the runner and its manifest), github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com (Git and 7-Zip), mcr.microsoft.com (the base image), and Docker Hub (the token proxy image). What needs internet lists everything. Not tested without internet access: Upgrade the runner on Windows.
  • Disk: servercore is about 2.2 GB compressed. Each container shows 20 GB free on C: by default. To raise the limit, add "storage-opts": ["size=60GB"] to C:\ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json. Every finished container keeps its layer until Swarm prunes it.
  • CPU and memory for the services, and runner concurrency in your CircleCI plan for your replicas (Size the limits).
Windows Server Machine runner 3 Status in this repository
2025 Compatible Tested in CI, image tag ltsc2025
2022 Compatible Tested in CI, image tag ltsc2022
2019 Compatible Untested here: the stack files have no label or placement for it
2016 and older Not compatible Not supported

Image tags and host builds

With process isolation, the image build must be the host build or an older one. Label every node with the image tags it can run: a service is placed on a node that carries the label of its image tag.

Host Images it can run Node labels
Windows Server 2022 ltsc2022 only machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true
Windows Server 2025 ltsc2025 and ltsc2022 machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true and machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true

The shipped services use ltsc2022 images, so they run on 2022 and 2025 nodes. A service on an ltsc2025 image requires machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 == true, so it runs on 2025 nodes only. A mismatch that the labels do not catch fails with 0xc0370101.

Self-hosted runner terms agreement

An organization admin must agree to the CircleCI Runner Terms before you install self-hosted runners through the web app. Through the CLI, you agree by installing and using them (details). Whether the token proxy between your runners and CircleCI is covered is for your own review: this project does not give legal advice.

Get the files

Use a release (recommended) or clone the repository at a release tag. Paths on this page are relative to the root of either. The GitHub release has the bundle machine-runner-swarm-<version>.zip, and the Linux page lists every file of a release.

git clone --branch <release-tag> https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm.git
cd machine-runner-swarm

Install cosign

cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x verifies the release (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). Download the executable and the checksum list of the cosign release, compare the checksum, and put the file in a directory on your PATH:

$cosign = '3.1.3'
$u = "https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/download/v$cosign"
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$u/cosign-windows-amd64.exe" -OutFile cosign.exe
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$u/cosign_checksums.txt" -OutFile cosign_checksums.txt
$want = ((Get-Content cosign_checksums.txt | Where-Object { $_ -match '\scosign-windows-amd64\.exe$' }) -split '\s+')[0]
if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath cosign.exe).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw 'the checksum of cosign.exe does not match: stop' }
.\cosign.exe version

This checks the file against a list from the same place: it catches a damaged download, not a compromised release page. Your own package manager is another source.

Verify a release

CircleCI signs the file SHA256SUMS of each release with the OIDC token of the job that makes the release. The signature proves that a job of this CircleCI project made the file, and the checksum proves that your download is the file that the job made. The Linux page explains what the signature proves, and what it does not.

Set $version once to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The download fails while the placeholder is unchanged.

$version = 'X.Y.Z'
$base = "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v$version"
$zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip"

Then paste this block. It stops at the first failing check. The variables are set outside it, because & runs the block in a scope of its own. Only a bundle that passes the signature, the ref and the checksum is unpacked.

& {
 $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
 foreach ($f in $zip, 'SHA256SUMS', 'SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json') { Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$base/$f" -OutFile $f }

 # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS
 cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json `
 --certificate-identity 'https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60' `
 --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://oidc.circleci.com'
 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'the signature does not verify: stop' }

 # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main
 # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main)
 $material = (Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | ConvertFrom-Json).verificationMaterial
 if ($material.certificate) { $cert = $material.certificate.rawBytes } else { $cert = $material.x509CertificateChain.certificates[0].rawBytes }
 $hex = -join ([Convert]::FromBase64String($cert) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') })
 if ($hex -notmatch '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e') { throw 'NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop' }

 # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list
 $want = ((Get-Content SHA256SUMS | Where-Object { $_ -match "\s$([regex]::Escape($zip))$" }) -split '\s+')[0]
 if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $zip).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw "the checksum of $zip is not the signed one: stop" }

 # only a verified bundle is unpacked
 Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath .
 'RELEASE VERIFIED'
}

Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files, and start again or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block reads the certificate extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) and fails unless its value is refs/heads/main. The pattern starts on a byte boundary, and ASN.1 tag 0c or 13 is the string type of the value.

Then change into the bundle:

cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version"

The token proxy image has its own signature: Verify the token proxy image has the commands.

The token proxy image

The token proxy holds your class tokens (The token proxy). On Windows it is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy of Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs), which the stack file token-proxy-windows pulls on deploy: a static binary on Nano Server, for windows/amd64. The name is not the trust root: the signature check is. One tag also holds the Linux images, and a manifest list holds one Windows image for Server 2022 and one for Server 2025, so Docker picks the one of the host. Tags, pinning and the signature are the same as on Linux: The token proxy image and Verify the token proxy image.

The image runs as ContainerAdministrator, as the stock Server Core image does, because ContainerUser of Nano Server cannot write to the volume that keeps the state of the proxy.

There is no windows/arm64 image, because CI has no Windows on Arm host to build and test one on. In a cluster with Windows on Arm nodes, pin the proxy to a windows/amd64 node with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT (Multi-Node Clusters). A cluster of only Windows on Arm nodes needs an image of your own: build the proxy with GOARCH=arm64, build proxy\Dockerfile.windows on an arm64 host with an arm64 Nano Server image as --build-arg BASE=, and name it with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE.

To use another image (development, an air gap), set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE in the environment of docker stack deploy. The image must be on the node that runs the proxy: a local build exists only where you built it. This builds one from a checkout: build the binary on any host with Go, then build the image on the Windows host whose build matches the base image.

$env:GOOS = 'windows'; $env:GOARCH = 'amd64'; $env:CGO_ENABLED = '0'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path build | Out-Null
Push-Location proxy; go build -trimpath -o ..\build\machine-runner-swarm-proxy.exe .\cmd\machine-runner-swarm-proxy; Pop-Location
docker build -f proxy\Dockerfile.windows -t machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev build
$env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE = 'machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev'

1. Create the resource classes

  1. Create a namespace if your organization has none.

    circleci namespace create <namespace> --org <org>

  2. Create one resource class for each service in the stack files. The class name must equal the service name. The shipped windows\stack\runners.yaml has the service windows-default and deploys on its own.

    circleci runner resource-class create <namespace>/windows-default --org <org> --generate-token

The command prints the token once: store it in your secret manager. The optional add-on files in the same directory add windows-custom (custom-image.yaml), windows-persistent (persistent.yaml), windows-docker-build (docker-build.yaml) and windows-default-ssh (ssh-rerun.yaml, untested). Create the classes you plan to use.

2. Prepare each host

Run these steps in an elevated PowerShell on every host, before you start Swarm: the network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init, and the pull needs it.

  1. Confirm that Docker runs Windows containers. The command prints windows.

    docker info --format '{{.OSType}}'

  2. Pull the base image of the shipped services once, so the first task does not wait for it. A Server 2025 host runs ltsc2022 images too, so this is the image for both hosts. Pull ltsc2025 as well only for a service that you put on that image.

    docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022

  3. On the host that runs the token proxy (a manager, by default), pull its image too, or build your own (The token proxy image).

    docker pull ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:latest

3. Start Swarm and label the node

  1. On the first host, start Swarm. Always pass --advertise-addr with the IPv4 address of the host: a plain docker swarm init fails on some hosts with could not find the system's IP address. For more than one node, see Multi-Node Clusters.

    docker swarm init --advertise-addr <host IPv4 address>

  2. Label the node with the image tags it can run. A Server 2022 node gets the first label, and a Server 2025 node gets both.

    docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true <node name>
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true <node name>

On a single node, the token proxy needs no label: it runs on the manager, and the jobs run there too. In a cluster, give the proxy a node of its own: label it machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true, and runner services never run there, so a job never shares a node with the proxy. Do not set the label on the only node of a swarm, because no runner would be placed. If the managers are Linux hosts, or there are several managers, also pin the proxy to a Windows node with the placement in the environment of docker stack deploy:

docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <node name>
$env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT = 'node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true'

Without a matching node the proxy stays pending and no runner can claim (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). The optional classes need one more label each, on the nodes that run them:

Class Label
windows-docker-build machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true
windows-persistent machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true

4. Create the secrets

Create one secret for each service you deploy, named <service>-token, including each optional class (windows-persistent-token too: persistent.yaml declares it as external, so the deploy fails without it). It is a runner config file that holds only the token:

api:
 auth_token: <token>

The token proxy mounts the secrets of the proxied classes, and those runners never see them. The persistent class is the exception (The persistent class). The runners read one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token in the same format (the setup helper creates it). Swarm mounts it at C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml, and the runner reads it with --config. Every other runner setting is a CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* variable in the stack file.

This block asks for the token with hidden input and passes the config to docker secret create on stdin, so no file with the token is written on the host. Repeat the first part for each class, with its name in $class. Create the placeholder once.

$class = 'windows-default'
$secure = Read-Host -Prompt "Runner token for $class" -AsSecureString
$bstr = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($secure)
try { $token = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringBSTR($bstr) } finally { [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($bstr) }
if (-not $token) { throw "no token entered for $class" }
"api:`n auth_token: $token`n" | docker secret create "$class-token" -
Remove-Variable token
"api:`n auth_token: machine-runner-swarm-placeholder`n" | docker secret create runner-placeholder-token -

Windows does not support the uid, gid and mode options of secrets: only administrators and SYSTEM can read the file inside the container, and jobs run as an administrator. Swarm also writes the secret in clear text to the disk of the container until it stops, which is a Swarm limitation on Windows (Linux keeps it in memory). Enable BitLocker on the Docker volume (Token model on each OS).

5. Review the stack files

Copy windows\stack to a directory of your own, deploy\, and keep it under version control. From here on you check and deploy your copies and never the files under windows\stack. For a first run, change nothing.

Copy-Item -Recurse windows\stack deploy

Check that the file parses. This needs no running Swarm.

docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml | Out-Null

The directory holds the stack files and runner-distributor.ps1, the script that runners.yaml ships as a Swarm config (file: runner-distributor.ps1): keep it next to runners.yaml. Review these first (Resource Classes has the details):

Service File Purpose
runner-distributor-windows runners.yaml Installs and upgrades the runner and Git on every Windows node. Keep it in your copy
windows-default runners.yaml Stock Server Core image, two replicas
windows-custom custom-image.yaml Your own image on top of stock Server Core (Images). It has a placeholder image that you replace
windows-persistent persistent.yaml A long-lived runner with a named volume (Persistent mode)
windows-docker-build docker-build.yaml Builds Windows images with the host engine (Docker Builds)
windows-default-ssh ssh-rerun.yaml Rerun job with SSH, port 54782. Untested on Windows (Rerun job with SSH)
  • runners.yaml needs the secrets windows-default-token and runner-placeholder-token. Each add-on file needs its own <service>-token.
  • The distributor settings (the runner version, a mirror, an explicit SHA-256 list) are variables of docker stack deploy and need no edit (Upgrade the runner on Windows).
  • For a class on the ltsc2025 image, copy a service under a new name and resource class, use the ltsc2025 image tag, and set the constraint node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 == true.
  • Add each optional file with another -c flag, and pass the same list on every deploy (how the files merge). Each add-on file repeats the anchors of runners.yaml and declares the volume runner-bin, so it also loads alone: change a common setting in every file you use.

To check the optional files, pass them all in the order you deploy them:

docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\custom-image.yaml -c deploy\persistent.yaml -c deploy\docker-build.yaml | Out-Null

For the keys that Windows honours and ignores, see Stack keys on Windows.

6. Deploy the stack

Deploy your copy from step 5:

docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners

To add optional classes, pass your copies after runners.yaml with more -c flags, for example your own image on top of stock Server Core:

docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\custom-image.yaml runners

This is the whole install: nothing is staged on the host. The service runner-distributor-windows starts on every Windows node, downloads the pinned runner version (the newest that CI tests) and the pinned portable Git (about 60 MB, 406 MB unpacked), verifies their SHA-256 checksums (the runner against the values the stack file carries, not CircleCI’s manifest), installs them into the per-node volume runner-bin, and flips two links. The runner services mount the volume read-only twice: current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, where the task agent expects tar.exe. The stock Server Core image needs no changes, and circleci-runner.exe is the main process of the container.

On a new node the first runner tasks fail with cannot access path ... \current until the distributor has flipped the link, which takes a few minutes for the first download. Swarm starts the next task after the restart delay of 10 seconds, so nothing needs to be done. Watch the distributor:

docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows

Verify the deployment

  1. List the services and tasks. The service runners_runner-distributor-windows shows one replica for each Windows node.

    docker stack services runners
docker stack ps runners --no-trunc

  2. Check that the runners connected. Each replica is listed as online, named <node hostname>-<service>-<slot>. The web app shows the same under Runners.

    circleci runner instance list --org <org> --resource-class <namespace>/windows-default

  3. Run a job. The quickstart has a complete config, and examples/windows-job.yml has more steps. Run the workflow twice: the two runs print different values for $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID, because each job runs in a new container.

What jobs can use

  • The default shell is Git Bash (bash -eo pipefail). Set shell: powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass for Windows PowerShell 5.1, or shell: cmd.exe, per job or step.
  • The working directory is C:\cci\w, and the task agent lives in C:\cci\agent. The PATH of the service reaches every step.
  • checkout, caches, test results and artifacts need Git and outbound access. Workspaces use the tar and gzip from the mounted Git.
  • OpenID Connect tokens need a writable %TEMP%.
  • The stack enables Git long paths through the environment. The registry value LongPathsEnabled is not set: a job that needs long paths for other tools sets it itself, or in its own image.
  • Not supported: desktop or UI automation, Docker commands in jobs (except the opt-in docker-build class), and service containers.
  • Not tested: add_ssh_keys, Hyper-V isolation, group managed service accounts, and proxies.
  • MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER of the Linux entrypoint do not exist on Windows, and Windows ignores them. There is no step-down.

Optional: use the setup helper

windows\Setup.ps1 checks the host, starts Swarm on request, labels the node, creates the secrets, and deploys. It does not install the runner: the distributor service of the stack does that on every node. It runs in an elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session and is safe to run again. It prints CHECK <name> PASS or FAIL for each preflight check (administrator, Windows Server build, Windows-container mode, Docker 28.0 or later, Swarm manager), and ends with Next: and the steps still to do, or Check: and the commands that watch the start.

Parameter Effect
-InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr <ip> Creates a Swarm when none exists, and waits until the node is a manager. The address is needed only then: on an active Swarm, -InitSwarm changes nothing
-Class <name>,<name> Asks for each token with hidden input and creates the secret <name>-token. An existing secret stays unchanged
(placeholder) With -Class or -Deploy, it also creates the secret runner-placeholder-token with a made-up token, which every runner reads
-Deploy Runs docker stack deploy with -StackFile (one or more files, runners.yaml first) and -StackName (default runners). Without -StackFile it deploys the shipped windows\stack\runners.yaml as it is, which suits a first run. Once you keep copies as in step 5, pass them. It prints the files it deploys

The helper labels the node from the host build: windows-ltsc2022=true on Server 2022, and both windows-ltsc2022=true and windows-ltsc2025=true on Server 2025 (machine-runner-swarm. prefix). It supports Server 2022 and 2025 only, and does not add the labels of the optional classes. The distributor reads its settings from the environment of -Deploy.

The first command is a first run with the shipped runners.yaml. The second deploys your copy from step 5, with its optional file.

.\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr 10.0.0.5 -Class windows-default -Deploy
.\windows\Setup.ps1 -Class windows-default,windows-custom -StackFile .\deploy\runners.yaml,.\deploy\custom-image.yaml -Deploy

Upgrade

The distributor pins the exact runner version that this release tests, with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, and the nodes keep it until you change it. 3.1, 3 or current (weaker: they trust the hash of the manifest) follow CircleCI’s manifest and check every 24 hours. A pin of your own is two variables of docker stack deploy: the version and its SHA-256 values (or manifest for an exact version without a list). Running jobs keep their version, and the runner services never restart (Upgrade the runner on Windows).

A new release of this repository changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy\ is not updated by itself. To merge, with git from Git for Windows or another diff and merge tool:

  1. Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.

  2. Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old directory is the base of the merge.

  3. See what changed between the two releases, and merge each file that differs into your copy. git merge-file edits the file in place, marks conflicts with <<<<<<< lines, and exits with the number of conflicts.

    git diff --no-index "machine-runner-swarm-$old\windows\stack" "machine-runner-swarm-$new\windows\stack"
git merge-file deploy\runners.yaml "machine-runner-swarm-$old\windows\stack\runners.yaml" "machine-runner-swarm-$new\windows\stack\runners.yaml"

    Repeat for the other files you copied. Take runner-distributor.ps1 of the new release unless you edited it (Upgrade to a new release of this repository explains the names of the Swarm configs).

  4. Check deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints and deploy.resources, the runner version pin with its SHA-256 values (a release changes them together), and the token proxy image (a release names it by digest).

  5. Check the result.

    docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml | Out-Null

  6. Deploy while the classes are idle (Stop a busy Windows container), with the same list of -c files as before.

    docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners

To roll back, deploy the previous copy.

Stop and uninstall

Refer to Uninstall. Every stop of a busy service kills its job after about 5 seconds. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.

Troubleshooting

Refer to Troubleshooting. The most common problems are an image tag that does not match the host build, a distributor that has not installed the runner yet, and a job that ends about 5 seconds after a stop. A task also stays pending when no node carries the machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 label (or windows-ltsc2025, for a service on an ltsc2025 image).

Additional resources

  • Concepts
  • Resource Classes
  • Security
  • Operations
  • Machine runner 3 on Windows

item.title: Multi-node clusters
item.description:
This page runs the stack on a cluster of Linux amd64, Linux arm64 and Windows nodes. One Swarm schedules every replica, and labels decide which node may run which resource class.

Start with the single-node steps on Install on Linux with Docker Swarm or Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm, then use this page to add nodes.

flowchart LR
subgraph nodes["Nodes and their labels"]
A["linux-a<br/>linux, x86_64<br/>machine-runner-swarm.zone=build"]
B["linux-b<br/>linux, aarch64<br/>machine-runner-swarm.zone=build"]
C["linux-c<br/>linux, x86_64<br/>machine-runner-swarm.zone=deploy"]
D["linux-d (worker)<br/>linux, x86_64<br/>machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true"]
W["win-a<br/>windows<br/>machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true"]
end
subgraph services["Services and their constraints"]
S1["linux-build<br/>os == linux<br/>zone == build"]
S2["linux-arm64<br/>arch == aarch64"]
S3["linux-deploy<br/>zone == deploy"]
S4["linux-docker-build<br/>role == worker<br/>docker-build == true"]
S5["windows-default<br/>os == windows<br/>machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 == true"]
end
S1 -.-> A
S1 -.-> B
S2 -.-> B
S3 -.-> C
S4 -.-> D
S5 -.-> W

A dotted line means that the node satisfies every constraint of the service, so Swarm may place a replica there. A service stays pending when no node matches.

Plan the cluster

Node type Role Needs
Manager Holds the cluster state and every secret. Schedules tasks Docker Engine. Linux managers can manage Windows workers
Linux worker Runs Linux services Docker Engine. The runner-distributor service installs the runner for the architecture of the node
Windows worker Runs Windows services Docker Engine in Windows-container mode, the ltsc2022 base image, the machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc* labels. Nothing else: the distributor installs the runner and Git

Managers and quorum

Managers keep the cluster state, including every Swarm secret, in an encrypted Raft log. Each manager holds a copy.

  • Use one manager for a small installation without availability needs, three to survive the loss of one, or five to survive the loss of two. Use an odd number: quorum is a majority.
  • Keep the managers on reliable, low-latency links.

Quorum matters more here than in a typical Swarm. Every job ends with a runner exit, and only a manager with quorum can create the replacement task. Without quorum, running jobs finish but the runners are not replaced, so the capacity drops to zero.

Keep jobs off managers when you can: a container breakout on a manager exposes the tokens of every class. In a cluster, label the node that runs the token proxy (a manager) and tell the deploy about it. Runner services never run on a node with that label, so no job shares a node with the class tokens.

docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <manager name>
sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

Keep the variable with your other deploy variables (Keep the deploy variables in version control): a deploy without it puts the proxy back on any manager. Drain the other managers so that they run no tasks.

docker node update --availability drain <other manager name>

Warning

The token proxy needs a node that is not drained. token-proxy runs on a manager by default (node.role == manager), or on the labeled node. If you drain every manager, or the labeled node, the proxy stays Pending (no suitable node) and no runner can claim a job, with no other error: the runners only log 502 or a refused connection to token-proxy. The same happens when the managers are Linux hosts and the proxy is the Windows one (token-proxy-windows also defaults to a manager, and a Windows task cannot run on a Linux manager), and when a Windows-only swarm has no Windows manager. Label a Windows node for it (a worker works), and in a mixed cluster label one Linux and one Windows node, because each proxy keeps to its own operating system. Never drain the labeled node without the steps in The node of the proxy. A proxy on a worker still holds every class token, so choose a node that runs no jobs.

On a single-node Swarm the only node is a manager and runs the replicas and the proxy: set no label. Never use the Docker socket classes (pattern A) there (Docker Builds).

Create the swarm

Initialize Swarm on the first manager with an address that the other nodes can reach (not the loopback address of the single-node install).

docker swarm init --advertise-addr <manager IP address> --task-history-limit 2 --default-addr-pool 10.20.0.0/16 --default-addr-pool-mask-length 24

Two options matter for this stack, and neither is the default:

  • --task-history-limit 2. Every finished job ends a task, and Swarm keeps the last 5 tasks of each slot, with their containers and disk, unless you lower it (Free disk space). Change it later with docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2.
  • --default-addr-pool. Each Linux class gets its own /24 overlay network from the default pool of Swarm, 10.0.0.0/8. Choose a pool that does not overlap your own networks, because an overlap makes tasks unreachable in ways that are hard to see. A /16 gives 256 networks. You can set the pool only when you create the swarm.

If you started with the loopback address, run docker stack rm runners and docker swarm leave --force, initialize again, and recreate the secrets.

Get the join command for each node type on a manager. Run the printed command (docker swarm join --token <token> <manager IP address>:2377) on the node.

docker swarm join-token worker
docker swarm join-token manager

A join token grants cluster membership: keep it secret, and rotate it with docker swarm join-token --rotate worker when it leaks. Confirm the nodes from a manager.

docker node ls

Join the nodes

Linux nodes

On each node:

  1. Install Docker Engine and confirm that the clock is synchronized (Prepare each node).
  2. Open the ports in Inter-node ports.
  3. Run the join command.

Nothing else is installed on the node. The runner-distributor service is global, so Swarm starts it on the new node by itself, and it installs the runner into the volume runner-bin (it skips a node labeled machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true: the microVM classes download their own runner). A runner container that starts first waits up to 120 seconds for it.

Arm nodes

The runner-distributor service reads the architecture of the node and installs the arm64 runner build on an Arm node. Swarm reports Arm nodes as aarch64 and Intel and AMD nodes as x86_64.

  • Give each architecture its own resource class, for example linux-arm64, constrained with node.platform.arch == aarch64: a job cannot pick an architecture inside a class that spans both.
  • Use an image that publishes an arm64 variant (check with docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>).

Mixed architectures

One cluster can have x86_64 and aarch64 nodes. Nothing else is needed on the nodes.

  • Which build a node gets. Each runner-distributor task downloads circleci-runner_linux_<arch>.tar.gz for its own node and checks its SHA-256 against the entry of that architecture in the manifest. If you set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256, list the hash of every architecture in the cluster. A tarball that does not match installs nothing on that node, and the other nodes still install.
  • Placement. A class without an architecture constraint can run on both kinds of node. Add node.platform.arch == aarch64 or x86_64 to the constraints of the classes that need one. When the nodes of that architecture are drained or gone, the class stays Pending with no suitable node: it never moves to the other architecture.
  • What is tested. linux/tests/mixed-arch.sh (the optional CI job linux-mixed-arch, see CI) deploys the shipped stack file on an amd64 manager and an arm64 worker. It checks that each node installs the runner of its own architecture, that a tarball that does not match its manifest entry installs nothing on that node only, and that classes constrained by node.platform.arch run only on their architecture, also when the other node is drained.
  • Emulated, not real. That arm64 worker is a docker:dind container under QEMU emulation on an x86_64 host. The test proves the install, the verification and the placement logic, not the speed or system call behavior of an Arm node. IPsec on overlays does not work under emulation, so it deploys the plain-overlay copy of the stack files (the opt-out of Encrypted class networks), and placement.sh tests the encrypted files on two nodes. Real arm64 nodes are tested by the single-node jobs linux-arm64 and e2e-linux-arm64 (a real runner on an Arm VM).

Windows nodes

On each node:

  1. Install Docker Engine in Windows-container mode and the Windows Containers feature.

  2. Pull the images before the join (Prepare each host). The runner and Git are not staged: the service runner-distributor-windows installs them after the join.

  3. Open the ports in Inter-node ports.

  4. Run the join command.

  5. From a manager, label the node with the image tags it can run. A Server 2025 node also gets windows-ltsc2025, because it runs ltsc2022 images too.

    docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true <node name>
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true <node name>

The labels are required, because the image build must be the host build or an older one (Image tags and host builds).

Deploy the Linux and Windows files into the same stack name. The service names differ, so they do not collide. Do not use docker stack deploy --prune there: it removes the services of the other file.

Mixed Linux and Windows clusters are tested by hand, not in CI. The constraints on node.platform.os keep each service on its own operating system. A cluster of a Linux manager and a Windows Server 2022 worker ran real CircleCI jobs on both operating systems, with both runner distributors and an overlay network between them. CI tests each operating system on its own Swarm, because the Linux and Windows VMs of CI cannot reach each other. A mixed cluster needs the ports 2377, 7946 and 4789 open between its nodes (Inter-node ports), and a Linux manager that both stack files are deployed from.

Labels and constraints

A service constraint says where Swarm may place a replica, and all constraints of a service must hold. Add them under deploy.placement.constraints. The spread: node.id preference, which the shipped stack files set, spreads the replicas evenly over the matching nodes.

deploy:
 placement:
 constraints:
 - node.platform.os == linux
 - node.platform.arch == aarch64
 - node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.zone == build
 preferences:
 - spread: node.id

Built-in node properties

Property Values
node.platform.os linux, windows
node.platform.arch x86_64, aarch64
node.hostname The hostname of the node
node.role manager, worker

Labels used by this repository

Set a label with docker node update --label-add <key>=<value> <node name>, and remove it with --label-rm <key>. Constraints on labels have the form node.labels.<key> == <value>.

Label Value Used by
machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 true Every shipped Windows service, which uses ltsc2022 images. Set on Server 2022 and 2025 nodes
machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 true Services on an ltsc2025 image. Set on Server 2025 nodes only
machine-runner-swarm.zone A network zone name Services that must run in one zone. A commented example sits in the Linux placement block
machine-runner-swarm.docker-build true The docker-build services (pattern A) (Docker Builds)
machine-runner-swarm.container-mode true The container agent of container mode (experimental), on workers only. The token proxy stays off container-mode nodes
machine-runner-swarm.proxy true The node that runs the token proxy, in a cluster. With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' the proxy runs only there, and no runner service runs on a node with this label. On a single node, set no label (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves)
machine-runner-swarm.microvm true The microVM services, on nodes whose Docker daemon runs every container in a Kata microVM. Every other service stays off these nodes (MicroVM jobs)
machine-runner-swarm.class.<service> true Pins a service to the labeled nodes. windows-persistent uses machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent. linux-persistent pins itself with node.hostname instead

Keep the docker-build node to itself

A job on a docker-build class controls the whole Docker engine of its node, so it can enter every other container there and read the tokens of any class that runs on that node. The stack files keep the other classes off that node: every runner service except the docker-build ones carries the constraint node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.docker-build != true (a node without the label matches it, because Swarm treats a missing label as “not equal”). runner-distributor has no such constraint, because the docker-build class needs the runner on its node too. A node that gets the label stops running those services: Swarm starts replacements on other nodes, or leaves them pending. Add the same constraint to every service you write yourself.

Network zones

Use the label machine-runner-swarm.zone when your nodes sit in different network zones, for example a build network and a deploy network with different firewall rules or egress addresses.

  1. Label each node with its zone.

    docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.zone=build linux-a
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.zone=deploy linux-c

  2. Copy a service for each zone, give each copy its own resource class, secret and name, and add the constraint.

    linux-deploy:
 # ...
 deploy:
 placement:
 constraints:
 - node.platform.os == linux
 - node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.zone == deploy

A job picks the zone by picking the resource class. Do not use zones to balance capacity: use replicas and spread.

Registry needs

Swarm does not share images between nodes: each node pulls the image of a task from a registry the first time the task lands there.

  • Every node must reach the registry of every image that a service on that node uses (Egress hosts). Your own image must be in a registry that all nodes of its OS can reach (Images).
  • For a private registry, run docker login on the manager and deploy with docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth.
  • Pin images by digest, for example cimg/base:2026.10@sha256:<digest>, so every node runs the same content. Tags such as 21.0 move.
  • Pull large images ahead of time (a Windows servercore image is about 2.2 GB compressed). Public registries apply pull rate limits: a mirror or an authenticated pull avoids failed pulls.
  • runner-distributor runs the stock alpine:3 image on every Linux node. If the nodes cannot reach Docker Hub, mirror it and change image in your copy of the stack file. Copy it with its digest (docker buildx imagetools create keeps it), so the pin holds.
  • The token proxy runs from ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy. Mirror it with its signature (cosign copy), pin the digest in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE, and keep that in your deploy file (Upgrade the token proxy).
  • A manager that cannot reach the registry cannot resolve a tag to a digest on deploy. Use docker stack deploy --resolve-image never, or images that you pinned by digest and mirrored.
  • A site with no route to the internet also needs the runner download and the task agent (CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet).

Inter-node ports

Swarm needs these ports between all nodes of the cluster. Open them only for the addresses of cluster nodes.

Port Protocol Purpose Nodes
2377 TCP Cluster management Managers only receive it
7946 TCP and UDP Node discovery All nodes
4789 UDP Overlay network (VXLAN) All nodes
IP protocol 50 (ESP) IPsec Encrypted overlay networks (the Linux class networks). It is a protocol, not a port All nodes with Linux services

The runner containers need no inbound ports, and the stack publishes none. Outbound HTTPS from each node is the only other requirement (Egress hosts).

Ubuntu with ufw:

sudo ufw allow from <cluster subnet> to any port 2377 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow from <cluster subnet> to any port 7946
sudo ufw allow from <cluster subnet> to any port 4789 proto udp
sudo ufw allow from <cluster subnet> proto esp

RHEL with firewalld:

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --new-zone=swarm
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-source=<cluster subnet>
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-port=2377/tcp --add-port=7946/tcp --add-port=7946/udp --add-port=4789/udp
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-protocol=esp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

In a cloud, add a security group rule for protocol number 50 (ESP) with the security group of the nodes as the source. Most consoles list it as “Custom protocol 50” or “ESP”.

Windows Server:

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Swarm TCP' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 2377,7946 -RemoteAddress <cluster subnet>
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Swarm UDP' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol UDP -LocalPort 7946,4789 -RemoteAddress <cluster subnet>

On a Windows host with a single network adapter, an existing transparent network can block the creation of the overlay networks: see the Microsoft documentation on Windows container networking if overlay creation fails.

Encrypted class networks

The Linux stack files create the class networks as encrypted overlays: driver: overlay with driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"}. The runners reach the token proxy over http://token-proxy:8080, and that traffic carries task tokens, the job configuration with the secrets of its contexts, and step output. In clear text, anyone on the network could read it or inject packets into the overlay, which the source-address guarantee of the proxy depends on. Swarm encrypts the VXLAN traffic between nodes with IPsec instead. A node that cannot reach another over ESP drops that traffic, which looks like a runner that cannot find token-proxy: if a runner cannot reach the proxy from another node, check ESP first.

  • Cost. IPsec costs CPU on every node and some throughput. A single-node Swarm needs nothing open.
  • Opt out. If the network between your nodes is yours (a private network, or a link that you encrypt another way), delete driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"} from every class network of your copy of the Linux stack files (runners.yaml and the add-on files you use). A Swarm network cannot change after it exists: run docker stack rm runners, wait until the networks are gone (docker network ls), and deploy again. Without the option, ESP is not needed.
  • Windows. Docker does not support encrypted overlay networks for Windows containers, so the Windows stack files set no driver_opts, and their overlay carries the traffic of the Windows classes and token-proxy-windows in clear text between nodes. Keep the Windows nodes on a network that you trust, or encrypt the link at the host (for example with Windows Firewall connection security rules for IPsec). All Windows classes share the default overlay of the stack.

Verify the placement 

docker node ls
docker node inspect --format '{{ .Spec.Labels }}' <node name>
docker service ps runners_linux-default

The NODE column of docker service ps shows where each replica runs. A task that stays Pending shows the reason in the ERROR column, for example no suitable node (scheduling constraints not satisfied on 2 nodes) (A task stays pending).
